Understanding Diabetes

Learn about the types of diabetes, the factors that contribute to risk, and why early awareness matters.

What Is Diabetes?

Diabetes is a chronic condition that affects how the body processes glucose, the main type of sugar in the blood. When you eat, the body breaks food down into glucose, which enters the bloodstream. A hormone called insulin, produced by the pancreas, helps move glucose from the blood into cells where it is used for energy.

In diabetes, this process is disrupted. Either the body does not produce enough insulin, or it cannot use insulin effectively. As a result, glucose builds up in the blood instead of reaching the cells, leading to high blood sugar levels.

Over time, persistently high blood sugar can affect the heart, blood vessels, eyes, kidneys, and nerves. Understanding diabetes and its risk factors early can help individuals and healthcare professionals take appropriate steps toward better metabolic health.

Types of Diabetes

Click on each type to learn more about its characteristics

Diabetes

Type 1 Diabetes

An autoimmune condition where the body stops making enough insulin.

  • Often starts in childhood or adolescence
  • Requires lifelong insulin therapy
  • Early detection supports better management
Diabetes

Type 2 Diabetes

The body becomes less effective at using insulin and may gradually produce less over time.

  • Commonly linked to lifestyle and weight factors
  • Often develops gradually
  • Can be delayed or managed with lifestyle and clinical support
Diabetes

Gestational Diabetes

High blood sugar that develops during pregnancy and typically resolves after birth.

  • Can affect pregnancy health
  • May increase future diabetes risk
  • Monitoring and management are important during pregnancy

Diabetes Risk Factors

Explore the different categories of factors that contribute to diabetes risk

Biological

Age, family history, and weight

Some risk factors are built into a person’s health profile and may increase susceptibility over time.

Lifestyle

Activity, sleep, and nutrition

Daily patterns and habits can influence insulin sensitivity and metabolic health.

Clinical

Blood pressure, cholesterol, and prior labs

Clinical markers help clinicians understand risk in context rather than in isolation.

Environment

Stress, access, and social context

The broader environment can shape health outcomes and make risk more complex to interpret.
